text:
Čudnovate zgode inuša Hlapića 

Bio je neki mali cipelarski šegrt ili inuš, ki nije imao ni oca ni majke. Zvao se je Hlapić. 
Hlapić je bio malen kot lakat, a veseo kot ptica. Cijel dan je sidio u poderani hlača i črljenoj košulji na malom cipelarskom stolcu, ki je imao tri noge, i cijeli dan je zabijao cveke u čizme i šio cipele. Cijeli dan je fućkao i pjevao pri poslu. 
Hlapićev gospodar zvao se majstor Mrkonja, a bio je zao i strašan. Tako je bio velik, da mu je glava dosigala do plafona u njihovoj maloj sobi. Imao je guste, kuštrave vlase kot lav, a duge brke (mustaće) do ramena. Njegov glas bio je tako jak i gruban kot u medvida. 
Majstoru Mrkonji dogodila se je jedanput u životu velika žalost i nesrića, pa je odonda bio vrlo tvrdoga srca. Kakova se je nesrića dogodila majstoru Mrkonji, to će se istom mnogo kasnije iz ove knjige doznati. 
Majstor Mrkonja bio je ada tvrdoga srca i vrlo nepravičan, pa je psovao i vikao na Hlapića kad god je bio zlovoljan. 
Majstorica je bila jako dobra. I njoj se je dogodila ista žalost kot i majstoru Mrkonji. No ona je od te dobe postala još bolja i imala je vrlo dobro srce. Hlapića je jako ljubila. 
Ali i ona se je bojala majstora Mrkonje. Kad god je nosila Hlapiću friškoga kruha, uvijek ga je sakrivala pod pregaču, da majstor ne vidi, jer je majstor zapovidao, da se Hlapiću daje on tvrdi i stari kruh, a majstorica je znala, da Hlapić rado ji meki krušac. 
Hlapić je imao samo jedne poderane hlače i još jedne, ke mu je majstorica načinila od zelenoga sukna. To sukno je bilo ostalo od majstorove zelene pregače, pa je majstor zapovidao svojoj ženi, da načini od toga Hlapiću hlače. Hlapić je imao u ti hlača tako zelene noge kot žaba, zato ih nije rado nosio, jer su mu se drugi šegrti rugali. Majstor Mrkonja je zapovidao, da ih mora nositi u nedilju. Hlapić je bio uvijek dobre volje, ter kad je vidio da mora nositi te hlače, počeo se i sam šaliti. Kreketao je „kre-kre“ kot žaba, kad god si je oblikao zelene hlače. 
Kad su vidili drugi šegrti, da se Hlapić šali, nisu mu se već rugali, nego su se igrali s njim po nedilje i vrlo su ga ljubili. Samo majstor Mrkonja nije smio viditi, da se Hlapić igra, jer bi ga on odmah otirao domom. Tako je živio Hlapić kod majstora Mrkonje i nije mu bilo dobro. Ali on bi bio ipak bogzna kako dugo ostao ondje, da se nije dogodilo nešto, ča je Hlapića preveć ražalostilo.

space: A small shoemaker’s workroom where the orphan apprentice Hlapić spends his days making and repairing footwear; his three-legged stool and the low ceiling emphasize the cramped setting.
The household of master shoemaker Mrkonja and his wife, where work, meals, clothing, and the treatment of Hlapić are governed by the master’s commands.
An unspecified space where Hlapić plays with other apprentices on Sundays, away from Mrkonja’s watchful presence; the passage does not describe its physical surroundings.
time: An unspecified past, introduced through the storyteller’s formula that there once was a little shoemaker’s apprentice.
Repetitive working days marked by continuous shoemaking, whistling, and singing.
Sundays, when Hlapić must wear his green trousers and can play with other apprentices if Mrkonja does not see him.
An earlier, undisclosed misfortune shared by Mrkonja and his wife, after which he became hardhearted while she became still kinder.
A narrative threshold: the passage ends by announcing an event that will deeply distress Hlapić, while withholding what happens.
characters_or_voices: Hlapić, a very small orphan boy apprenticed to a shoemaker, wears torn trousers and a red shirt, works on a three-legged stool, and remains cheerful through singing, whistling, and playful humor despite mistreatment.

Master Mrkonja, Hlapić’s imposing employer, is described as reaching the ceiling, with thick, unruly lionlike hair, a mustache extending to his shoulders, and a loud, rough, bearlike voice. An unnamed sorrow precedes his harshness, unfair commands, and angry treatment of Hlapić.

Mrkonja’s wife, the kind mistress of the household, loves Hlapić and secretly brings him fresh bread beneath her apron. She fears her husband, although their shared sorrow has made her more compassionate rather than cruel.
The other apprentices initially mock Hlapić’s green trousers but stop when he jokes about them himself; they then play with him on Sundays and become fond of him.

An external, conversational storyteller describes the characters’ circumstances and feelings, judges Mrkonja’s behavior as unjust, and explicitly postpones explanations and events until later in the story.
motifs: Orphanhood and dependence: Hlapić has neither father nor mother and lives under the authority of the master who employs him.
Shoemaking and repetitive labor: boots, shoes, nails, and a small three-legged shoemaker’s stool define Hlapić’s daily work.
Smallness against overwhelming size: Hlapić is compared to an elbow in size, while Mrkonja’s head is said to reach the ceiling.
Cheerfulness under hardship: Hlapić whistles and sings while working despite poverty and unjust treatment.
Bread as deprivation and care: Mrkonja orders that Hlapić receive hard, stale bread, while his wife secretly gives him the soft, fresh bread he enjoys.
Clothing as necessity and exposure to ridicule: Hlapić owns torn trousers and a green pair made from fabric left over from Mrkonja’s apron; he must wear the green pair on Sundays.
Froglike green legs and playful croaking: Hlapić turns the mockery of his green trousers into a shared joke by making the sound 'kre-kre.'
Contrasting responses to sorrow: the same unnamed misfortune is followed by Mrkonja’s hardened heart and his wife’s increased kindness.
Hidden kindness and restricted play: the mistress conceals fresh bread beneath her apron, and Hlapić’s Sunday games must remain out of Mrkonja’s sight.
An undisclosed sorrow and an impending distressing event create unanswered questions about the household’s past and Hlapić’s future.
artistic_procedures: Vivid similes characterize the figures through familiar images: Hlapić is small as an elbow and cheerful as a bird; Mrkonja has hair like a lion and a voice like a bear; Hlapić’s green-clad legs resemble a frog’s.
Hyperbolic scale makes Mrkonja physically overwhelming: his head reaches the ceiling of the small room, and his mustache extends to his shoulders.
Contrasts organize the portrayal of relationships: small apprentice versus enormous master, cheerful song versus angry shouting, stale bread versus fresh bread, and cruelty versus compassion.
Repetition of 'all day' emphasizes the duration and monotony of Hlapić’s labor while also sustaining the rhythm of his singing and whistling.
Concrete colors and objects make the scene visually distinctive: a red shirt, green trousers, torn fabric, an apron concealing bread, footwear, nails, and a three-legged stool.
Onomatopoeia in Hlapić’s 'kre-kre' imitates a frog’s croak and turns an embarrassing garment into a source of humor and companionship.
Delayed disclosure withholds the nature of the couple’s earlier misfortune, while the closing announcement of a distressing event creates suspense.
Regional vocabulary and speech forms give the storytelling a distinctive spoken texture; the narrator also explains some terms through alternatives, such as the two words used for an apprentice.
atmosphere: Cramped and oppressive domestic life, shaped by relentless work, material deprivation, Mrkonja’s shouting, and fear of his authority.
Warmth and tenderness surrounding the mistress’s concealed gifts of fresh bread and her affection for Hlapić.
Playful resilience expressed through Hlapić’s songs, whistles, frog imitation, and growing friendship with the other apprentices.
Underlying sadness and anticipatory unease, created by orphanhood, an unexplained past misfortune, and the announcement of a coming distress.

elements_interpretation: The passage places a small, dependent child within a cramped world dominated by an oversized and unjust master. Clothing, bread, tools, and bodily proportions make unequal power visible through everyday details. Yet Hlapić’s singing and frog imitation preserve his capacity for pleasure and transform ridicule into companionship, while the mistress’s hidden bread offers practical care within a fearful household. The couple’s contrasting responses to the same sorrow suggest that suffering does not inevitably produce cruelty. The atmosphere therefore combines oppression with tenderness and comic resilience. Withholding both the earlier misfortune and the coming distress positions this introduction at the threshold of a change whose precise form remains unknown.

illustration.interpretation:
The illustration gathers the household’s unequal relationships into a cramped shoemaker’s workroom. Hlapić sits on a small three-legged stool, holding a boot and drawing thread through it; shoes, nails, leather, and worn wooden surfaces surround him with the material demands of daily labor. His faded red shirt and patched green trousers make poverty immediately visible, bringing together clothing motifs that the text associates with different occasions. Behind him, Mrkonja stands with hands on hips, his broad body, spreading mustache, and head close to the low ceiling translating the storyteller’s exaggerations into an imposing physical presence. The crowded composition leaves little space beyond his authority.

Against this looming figure, the mistress bends toward Hlapić with bread gathered in her apron. Her lowered posture and his upward smile create an intimate exchange of care within the oppressive room. The apron recalls her concealed generosity, although here the bread is visible to the viewer and the master stands nearby: secrecy becomes a fragile pocket of tenderness rather than complete separation from his watchfulness. Hlapić’s smile renders the cheerfulness that the text expresses through singing, whistling, and jokes, without making his hardship disappear. Warm daylight catches his face, the bread, and the work-worn surroundings, allowing deprivation and affection to occupy the same scene. Rather than depicting Sunday play or the story’s withheld sorrows, the illustration concentrates on the central contrast between overwhelming power and the small acts of kindness and resilience that persist beneath it.

animation.interpretation:
Hlapić sits on a low wooden stool in a worn shoemaker’s workroom, holding a dark boot across his lap and working at it with small movements of his hand. His faded red shirt and trousers torn at the knee make the text’s material deprivation immediately visible, while the boots, scattered tools, small containers of nails, and shadowed shelves establish the repetitive world of his apprenticeship. From an absorbed, downward-looking posture, he gradually raises his head, rounds his lips as though whistling, and opens his mouth in a broad, singing smile. His eyes briefly close with pleasure before he lowers his gaze to the boot again. The returning sequence joins work and song into a recurring rhythm, giving visual form to the text’s repeated “all day.”

The animation concentrates on cheerfulness within hardship rather than depicting the household’s open conflicts. Mrkonja and his wife remain absent, so cruelty and concealed kindness are not enacted; instead, the contrast lies between the rough, confined surroundings and the boy’s expressive face. Warm light from the window catches his features, and the small green plant on the sill offers a possible visual echo of his vitality amid worn walls and dark leather. His upward glance momentarily loosens the bowed posture of labor without taking him away from his task. Returning to the boot does not erase his smile: the loop presents resilience not as escape from deprivation, but as a capacity to make room for pleasure within its repeated demands.
